explanations.explanation: That's what Isaiah says. These folks add house to house and join field to field until no place is left, and then they live alone in the land (Isaiah 5:8). Picture owning everything and having nobody to wave at from the porch. That's a whole lot of land for one set of footsteps.

Good guess, but the king never shows up in this verse. Isaiah says they keep going until no place is left, and then they live alone in the land (Isaiah 5:8). Nobody steps in to stop them. They just run out of land to grab.

Rain isn't in this verse at all, friend. Isaiah says they add house to house and join field to field until no place is left (Isaiah 5:8). The only thing that ends the shopping spree is running out of room. And then they live alone in the land.

Ooh, so close, but the LORD says the opposite. Isaiah hears Him declare that many houses will become desolate, and that great mansions will be left unoccupied (Isaiah 5:9). Empty is the word, not packed. Those mansions end up with plenty of room and nobody in it.

That's right. The LORD of Hosts says many houses will become desolate, and great mansions will be left unoccupied (Isaiah 5:9). Nobody is crowding in. Isaiah says he heard it himself, so he's passing it along just as he got it.
Yes, the grain. The LORD says a homer of seed will yield only an ephah of grain (Isaiah 5:10). That's the same bad news as the vineyard, just in the field. Plant a lot, get a little.

Olive oil is a fair guess for a farm, but it isn't in this verse. The LORD names the vineyard and the grain. A bath of wine from ten acres, and only an ephah of grain from a homer of seed (Isaiah 5:10).

Figs would make a fine harvest, but they're not mentioned here. The LORD says ten acres of vineyard will yield but a bath of wine. Then He says a homer of seed will yield only an ephah of grain (Isaiah 5:10). So the other short harvest is the grain.

explanations.answer: The work of the LORD's hands
explanations.explanation: That's it. Isaiah says they disregard the actions of the LORD and fail to see the work of His hands (Isaiah 5:12). The music is loud, and I think that's part of the problem. Hard to notice anything with a flute in your ear.

explanations.answer: The warnings of the city guards
explanations.explanation: City guards are a fair guess, but they never show up in this verse. Isaiah says these partiers disregard the actions of the LORD and fail to see the work of His hands (Isaiah 5:12). That's what they miss. The feast keeps their eyes on the table.

explanations.answer: The start of the harvest season
explanations.explanation: Harvest is on the farm side of this passage, not the feast side. At the feast, Isaiah says they disregard the actions of the LORD and fail to see the work of His hands (Isaiah 5:12). That's what slips right past them.

Yes. Isaiah says My people will go into exile for their lack of understanding (Isaiah 5:13). The word is understanding, and that's what's missing. I think that connects back to the feasts, where they didn't see the work of the LORD's hands (Isaiah 5:12).

Actually, it's true. Isaiah says My people will go into exile for their lack of understanding (Isaiah 5:13). Exile is what's coming, and understanding is what's missing. Easy one to flip, so no worries.

Right, it's Zion's. Isaiah says down go Zion's nobles and masses, her revelers and carousers (Isaiah 5:14). Zion is another name for Jerusalem, and those are the very people being warned. Nobles and regular folks alike go down together.

Egypt is a big name in the Bible, but it's not here. Isaiah says down go Zion's nobles and masses, her revelers and carousers (Isaiah 5:14). Zion is Jerusalem. This warning is aimed at God's own people.

Babylon is a fair guess for a prophet's warning, but not this time. Isaiah says it's Zion's nobles and masses, her revelers and carousers, who go down (Isaiah 5:14). Zion is Jerusalem. The people being warned are the ones at home.

That's the one. Isaiah says mankind will be brought low, each man humbled, and the arrogant will lower their eyes (Isaiah 5:15). Heads that were held high end up looking at the ground. I think that's a hard way to learn to look down.
The faithful aren't the ones lowering their eyes here. Isaiah says the arrogant will lower their eyes (Isaiah 5:15). They were the ones holding their heads high. Now they're looking at their shoes.

Watchmen are a good guess, since they watch for a living, but they're not in this verse. Isaiah says the arrogant will lower their eyes (Isaiah 5:15). Those are the proud ones, and they're the ones brought low.

Yes, exalted. Isaiah says the LORD of Hosts will be exalted by His justice, and the holy God will show Himself holy in righteousness (Isaiah 5:16). People get brought low, and He is lifted up. That's the contrast in the verse.

Silenced is the opposite of what the verse says. Isaiah says the LORD of Hosts will be exalted by His justice (Isaiah 5:16). Exalted means lifted high. The holy God will show Himself holy in righteousness.

Hidden doesn't fit, because the verse is about Him being seen. Isaiah says the LORD of Hosts will be exalted by His justice, and the holy God will show Himself holy in righteousness (Isaiah 5:16). Mankind goes low and He goes high.
That's right. Isaiah says strangers will feed in the ruins of the wealthy (Isaiah 5:17). The rich folks' fancy places turn into somebody else's dinner spot. Funny how fast the guest list changes.

This one's actually true. Isaiah says lambs will graze as in their own pastures, and strangers will feed in the ruins of the wealthy (Isaiah 5:17). The ruins belong to the wealthy, and strangers are the ones feeding there. It's a hard picture, but that's what the verse says.

explanations.answer: Let Him hurry so we can see it
explanations.explanation: Yes. They say, “Let Him hurry and hasten His work so that we may see it!” (Isaiah 5:19). Notice they say it while hauling sin on cart ropes (Isaiah 5:18). Asking for the show to start, with no plan to be in the right seat.

explanations.answer: Let Him wait until we repent
explanations.explanation: I wish they'd said that, friend. But they say the opposite: “Let Him hurry and hasten His work so that we may see it!” (Isaiah 5:19). Nobody in this verse mentions repenting. They're the ones asking for a hurry-up.

explanations.answer: Let Him keep it from the nations
explanations.explanation: The nations aren't part of what they say here. They say, “Let Him hurry and hasten His work so that we may see it!” (Isaiah 5:19). They want to see it for themselves. And they want it soon.

Yes. Isaiah says woe to those who call evil good and good evil (Isaiah 5:20). It sits right next to the darkness and light, and the bitter and sweet. It's all the same mix-up. Everything gets the wrong label.

It's true, actually. Isaiah says woe to those who call evil good and good evil (Isaiah 5:20). That's in the very same verse as turning darkness to light and light to darkness. Same woe, more examples.
That's right. Isaiah says woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight (Isaiah 5:21). They're the ones giving themselves the gold star. Nobody else handed it to them.

The king isn't named in this verse. Isaiah says woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight (Isaiah 5:21). It's their own opinion of themselves. Nobody else is doing the judging.

Elders are a fair guess, but they're not in this verse. Isaiah says woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight (Isaiah 5:21). The only judge here is the person looking in the mirror.
Yes, the guilty. Isaiah says they acquit the guilty for a bribe (Isaiah 5:23). Pay up and walk free. That's not justice, that's a price tag.
Priests aren't mentioned in this verse. Isaiah says they acquit the guilty for a bribe, and they deprive the innocent of justice (Isaiah 5:23). It's the guilty who walk free when money changes hands.
Foreigners aren't in this verse. Isaiah says these folks acquit the guilty for a bribe (Isaiah 5:23). That's who gets off. The bribe does the talking.
Not quite, friend. Isaiah says they deprive the innocent of justice (Isaiah 5:23). So the innocent are the ones getting shortchanged. The guilty walk free and the innocent lose out.

That's right. Isaiah says they acquit the guilty for a bribe and deprive the innocent of justice (Isaiah 5:23). The innocent don't get what they should. It's the reverse of what a judge is supposed to do.

Yes. Isaiah says they have rejected the instruction of the LORD of Hosts and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel (Isaiah 5:24). That's the reason he gives. The roots decay and the blossoms blow away like dust.

explanations.answer: They lost a long war with Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt isn't mentioned in this verse. Isaiah gives the reason himself: they have rejected the instruction of the LORD of Hosts and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel (Isaiah 5:24). It's about what they did with the LORD's word.

explanations.answer: They let their fields go unplanted
explanations.explanation: Fields do come up earlier in this passage, but not here. Isaiah's reason is that they have rejected the instruction of the LORD of Hosts and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel (Isaiah 5:24). The roots and blossoms are a picture, and the reason is the rejected word.

Not this time. Isaiah says that despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised (Isaiah 5:25). It's still burning and the hand is still raised. That's a heavy verse, and I think it's worth slowing down on.
That's right. Isaiah says, “Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.” (Isaiah 5:25). It's a heavy line, and I won't joke about it. The warning stays serious.
Yes, He whistles. Isaiah says He lifts a banner for the distant nations and whistles for those at the ends of the earth (Isaiah 5:26). No letter, no trumpet. One whistle, and they come.

No letter here, friend. Isaiah says He lifts a banner for the distant nations and whistles for those at the ends of the earth (Isaiah 5:26). It's a whistle that calls them. Nothing needs to be mailed.

A trumpet is a good guess, since a trumpet shows up in other parts of the Bible. But here Isaiah says He whistles for those at the ends of the earth (Isaiah 5:26). A banner goes up, and a whistle goes out.

It's the other way around. Isaiah says none of them grows weary or stumbles, and no belt is loose and no sandal strap is broken (Isaiah 5:27). Everything is fastened and ready. Not a loose strap in the bunch.
That's right. Isaiah says no belt is loose and no sandal strap is broken (Isaiah 5:27). He adds that none of them grows weary or stumbles. They come ready, with nothing hanging off.
Yes, no one. Isaiah says they growl and seize their prey, and carry it away, and no one can rescue it (Isaiah 5:29). That's the picture of a lion at work. Once it's taken, nobody can get it back.
The king isn't named in this verse. Isaiah says they carry it away, and no one can rescue it (Isaiah 5:29). Nobody at all can pull it back. That includes everybody, not just one person.
An army seems like a sensible answer, but the verse says no one can rescue it (Isaiah 5:29). That covers everybody, armies included. Once they seize their prey and carry it away, it's gone.
Yes. Isaiah says if one looks over the land, he will see darkness and distress (Isaiah 5:30). It's a heavy picture, and I think it's meant to be. The very last thing in this passage is a dark sky.
I'd love that ending, but it's not the one here. Isaiah says if one looks over the land, he will see darkness and distress (Isaiah 5:30). No harvest in view. Just a dim, hard scene.
Rebuilt walls would be a hopeful sight, but that's not what Isaiah says. If one looks over the land, he will see darkness and distress (Isaiah 5:30). That's the view at the end of this passage.
That's right. Isaiah says even the light will be obscured by clouds (Isaiah 5:30). Darkness and distress are on the land, and even the light is dimmed. A heavy ending, so I'll just let it sit.
Actually, it's true. Isaiah says even the light will be obscured by clouds (Isaiah 5:30). It comes right after he mentions darkness and distress. It's a heavy picture, and the verse says it plainly.
